propositions.text: Applicants are a family of four seeking temporary residence in Canada for the Principal Applicant's MBA studies.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are a family of four who sought to come to Canada to enable the Principal Applicant – Mr. Peyman Mohebban – to pursue his Masters in Business Administration.

propositions.text: Immigration Officer rejected applications for temporary residence, finding insufficient proof they would leave Canada after stay.
propositions.quote: An Immigration Officer [the Officer] rejected the applications for temporary residence, finding that they had not established that they would leave Canada at the end of their stay.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicants are a family seeking temporary residence for MBA studies; the Officer rejected their applications for insufficient proof of leaving Canada.

propositions.text: This application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, this application for judicial review is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application.

propositions.text: Applicants are Iranian citizens; Principal Applicant has degrees in engineering and construction management and is employed at NIGC since 2000.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are citizens of the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Principal Applicant has a Bachelor’s Degree in Planning and Systems Analysis in Industrial Engineering from the Islamic Azad University in Iran and a Master of Science in Construction Management from the Grenoble Graduate School of Business in France. He is currently the Head of Systems Analysis and Energy at the National Iranian Gas Company [NIGC] where he has been employed since October 7, 2000.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicants are Iranian citizens; the Principal Applicant has advanced degrees and long-term employment at NIGC.

propositions.text: Tetsaco offered Principal Applicant part-time Marketing Manager position; he may be promoted to Director of Engineering at NIGC upon return.
propositions.quote: Tetsaco International and Control [Tetsaco] is a private company that cooperates on some projects with NIGC. Tetsaco offered the Principal Applicant a position as a part-time Marketing Manager upon his return to Iran. The Principal Applicant also asserts that he is being considered for a promotion to Director of Engineering at NIGC upon his return.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Tetsaco offered the Principal Applicant a part-time job and he may get a promotion at NIGC upon return.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant admitted to MBA program in Vancouver, paid initial tuition deposit; total tuition is USD 54,975.
propositions.quote: He was admitted into the program on April 28 2022, and made an initial tuition deposit payment of $7,751.85. The overall tuition fees for the program are $54,975 United States dollars [USD].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Principal Applicant was admitted to an MBA program in Vancouver and paid initial tuition deposit.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant applied for study permit; spouse applied for work permit; daughters applied for study permit and visitor visa.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant subsequently applied for a study permit to allow him to pursue his MBA studies in Canada. To accompany him for the expected two-year duration of his studies, his spouse, Neda Torbatian [the Associate Applicant] applied for a work permit; his daughter, Dayana Mohebban applied for a study permit; and his second daughter, Andiya Mohebban, applied for a Visitor Visa.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Principal Applicant applied for a study permit and family members applied for accompanying permits.

propositions.text: Officer refused temporary residence applications on January 3, 2023, citing insufficient proof of leaving Canada due to financial, family ties, and purpose concerns.
propositions.quote: On January 3 2023, their applications for temporary residence in Canada were refused. In the decision letters, the Officer stated that the Principal Applicant had failed to establish that he would leave Canada at the end of his studies, due to the following factors: 1) his assets and financial situation were insufficient to support the stated purpose of travel; 2) he did not have significant family ties outside Canada; and 3) the purpose of the Principal Applicant’s visit to Canada was not consistent with a temporary stay given the details provided in his application.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer refused the applications citing insufficient assets, weak family ties outside Canada, and inconsistent purpose of visit.

propositions.text: Officer noted lack of detailed bank statements and unsatisfactory documentation of funds source, doubting sufficient funds for purpose.
propositions.quote: No detail bank statement/transaction submitted to check movement of funds on the account. In the absence of satisfactory documentation showing the source of these funds, I am not satisfied the PA has sufficient funds for the intended purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found no detailed bank statements and unsatisfactory proof of funds source, doubting sufficient funds.

propositions.text: Officer noted diminished motivation to return due to family accompanying, questioned MBA logic given prior degree, and found study cost unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Officer further notes that the Principal Applicant’s motivation to return to Iran would diminish since his spouse and two dependent children would be accompanying him to Canada. Additionally, the Officer considered the Principal Applicant’s desire to pursue an MBA in Canada illogical, noting that he already holds a Masters in Construction Management. The Officer also observed that the letter of offer submitted by the Principal Applicant was for part-time work and called into question whether international studies were required. The Officer concluded that the proposed course of study was unreasonable considering the high cost of international education in Canada. Together, these factors led the Officer to find that the Applicants had not established that they would depart Canada at the end of the period authorized for their stay.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found family accompaniment reduced return motivation, questioned MBA necessity, and deemed study cost unreasonable, leading to refusal.

propositions.text: Issues on judicial review relate to the Principal Applicant’s study permit decision, as family applications depend on it.
propositions.quote: As such, the issues that arise on this judicial review relate to this decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the judicial review issues relate to the Principal Applicant's study permit decision.

propositions.text: Issues are whether the Officer acted with procedural fairness and whether the refusal decision was reasonable.
propositions.quote: Expressed on a general level, the issues to consider on judicial review are as follows: 1.Did the Officer reject the Applicants’ applications in a manner that was procedurally unfair? 2.Was the Officer’s decision to refuse the applications reasonable?

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issues as procedural fairness and reasonableness of the Officer's refusal decision.

propositions.text: IRPA s.20(1)(b) requires foreign nationals to hold prescribed documents and prove they will leave Canada at end of authorized stay.
propositions.quote: Paragraph 20(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] provides that a foreign national wishing to enter or remain in Canada as a temporary resident must establish that they hold a visa or other document prescribed by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [IRPR] and will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA s.20(1)(b) requires foreign nationals to hold prescribed documents and prove they will leave Canada after authorized stay.

propositions.text: IRPR s.216(1) requires officers to issue study permits if applicant meets criteria including leaving Canada after stay and acceptance at designated institution.
propositions.quote: The following sections of the IRPR are relevant to the case at bar: Study permits 216 (1) Subject to subsections (2) and (3), an officer shall issue a study permit to a foreign national if, following an examination, it is established that the foreign national (a) applied for it in accordance with this Part; (b) will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay under Division 2 of Part 9; (c) meets the requirements of this Part; (d) meets the requirements of subsections 30(2) and (3), if they must submit to a medical examination under paragraph 16(2)(b) of the Act; and (e) has been accepted to undertake a program of study at a designated learning institution.

propositions.text: IRPR s.220 requires officers to refuse study permits unless applicant has sufficient financial resources for tuition, maintenance, and transport without working in Canada.
propositions.quote: Financial resources 220 An officer shall not issue a study permit to a foreign national, other than one described in paragraph 215(1)(d) or (e), unless they have sufficient and available financial resources, without working in Canada, to (a) pay the tuition fees for the course or program of studies that they intend to pursue; (b) maintain themself and any family members who are accompanying them during their proposed period of study; and (c) pay the costs of transporting themself and the family members referred to in paragraph (b) to and from Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPR s.216(1) and s.220 set criteria for study permits including leaving Canada and sufficient financial resources.

propositions.text: Fairness concerns on judicial review are reviewed on a correctness standard with no deference to the Officer.
propositions.quote: The fairness concerns raised by the Applicants are to be reviewed on a standard approximating the correctness standard: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54, and Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43.

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness issues are reviewed on a correctness standard with no deference to the Officer.

propositions.text: The standard of review on the substance of the Officer’s decision is reasonableness.
propositions.quote: On the substance of the Officer’s decision, there is no dispute between the parties that the applicable standard of review is reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, at para 25 [Vavilov]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the substantive standard of review is reasonableness.

propositions.text: A reasonable decision must show justification, transparency, intelligibility, and be based on a rational chain of analysis.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is one that displays justification, transparency and intelligibility with a focus on the decision actually made, including the justification for it: Vavilov at para 15. A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker: Vavilov at para 85.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a reasonable decision must be justified, transparent, intelligible, and rationally analyzed.

propositions.text: Visa officer decisions must be reasonable, based on coherent analysis, justified by facts and law, and show justification, transparency, intelligibility.
propositions.quote: The standard of review applicable to a review of a visa officer’s decision to refuse a study permit application is that of reasonableness…While it is not necessary to have exhaustive reasons for the decision to be reasonable given the enormous pressure on visa officers to produce a large volume of decisions each day, the decision must still be based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and be justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker…It must also bear “the hallmarks of reasonableness — justification, transparency and intelligibility” [citations omitted].

paragraphs.summary: The court states visa officer decisions must be reasonable, coherent, justified, transparent, and intelligible.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness owed to study permit applicants is low.
propositions.quote: It is well established that the level of procedural fairness owed to study permit applicants falls at the low end of the spectrum: Nourani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 732 at para 50; Patel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 517 at para 12.

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness owed to study permit applicants is low.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer breached procedural fairness by inadequate reasons, implicit credibility finding, no chance to respond, ignoring evidence.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that the Officer breached their rights to procedural fairness by failing to provide adequate reasons for the decision, by making an implicit credibility finding, by failing to allow the applicants to respond to their concerns, and by breaching the doctrine of legitimate expectations, by ignoring the evidence in the application.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue the Officer breached procedural fairness by inadequate reasons, implicit credibility finding, no response chance, and ignoring evidence.

propositions.text: Court rejects Applicants' procedural fairness arguments as similar to those rejected in Amiri case.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the Applicants made essentially identical arguments in another matter that recently came before this court: Amiri v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 1532 [Amiri]. In Amiri, Justice Ahmed succinctly considered, and rejected, these arguments as follows:

propositions.text: In Amiri, the Officer did not make an implicit credibility finding; refusal was based on evidence leading to conclusion Applicants would not leave Canada.
propositions.quote: The Applicants do not point to any evidence or jurisprudence to suggest that the Officer made an implicit credibility finding. Nowhere in the decision did the Officer maintain that the truth of the evidence or the Applicants’ statements were doubted. Rather, in both decisions the Officer found that the evidence led to the conclusion that the Applicants would not leave at the end of the period authorized for their stay.

propositions.text: Officer not required to inform applicants of concerns before rejecting claims (Kumar v Canada).
propositions.quote: As such, the Officer was not under a duty to inform the Applicants of concerns or considerations before rejecting their claims (Kumar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 935 at paras 18-19).

propositions.text: Doctrine of legitimate expectations irrelevant to procedural fairness; evidence consideration reviewed for reasonableness (Aje v Canada).
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Respondent is correct that the doctrine of legitimate expectations is irrelevant. The question of whether the Officer considered all of the evidence in a decision is a question relating to the reasons and conclusions of the decision itself, rather than the procedural steps followed by the officers throughout the applications. This consideration is reviewed for its reasonableness (Aje v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2022 FC 811 at paras 11-12). There has been no breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Applicants' procedural fairness arguments, citing Amiri case and legal principles that no implicit credibility finding or legitimate expectations breach occurred.

propositions.text: Adequacy of reasons is substantive review on reasonableness standard once some reasons are provided
propositions.quote: where some reasons for decision have been provided, the question of adequacy is no longer considered a matter of fairness. Rather, assessing adequacy goes to the content of the reasons provided and, as such, it calls for substantive review on the reasonableness standard

propositions.text: Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board) sets adequacy standard at para 14
propositions.quote: Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 14

propositions.text: Justice Ahmed’s reasoning in Amiri is directly applicable here
propositions.quote: I agree with Justice Ahmed’s reasoning in Amiri and find that it is directly applicable to the present case

paragraphs.summary: The court finds adequacy of reasons is reviewed on reasonableness standard citing Newfoundland Nurses' Union and agrees with Justice Ahmed's Amiri reasoning.

propositions.text: No indication Officer questioned Applicants’ credibility here
propositions.quote: there is no indication that the Officer questioned the Applicants’ credibility

propositions.text: Inadequate documentation of financial background is not a credibility finding absent other commentary
propositions.quote: A finding that an applicant has inadequately documented their financial background is not, absent other commentary from the decision-maker, a credibility finding

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no credibility question by Officer and inadequate financial documentation is not a credibility finding absent other commentary.

propositions.text: Officers have no legal obligation to clarify deficient applications or apprise applicants of concerns absent credibility issues or new info
propositions.quote: visa officers have no legal obligation to do what the Applicant suggests was necessary; that is, officers are not obliged to “seek to clarify a deficient application, to reach out and make the applicant’s case, to apprise an applicant of concerns relating to whether the requirements set out in the legislation have been met, or to provide the applicant with a running score at every step of the application process”

propositions.text: Solopova and Yuzer confirm no obligation on officers to clarify or assist applicants
propositions.quote: Solopova v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 690 at para 38; Yuzer v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 781 at para 16

propositions.text: This case does not require officers to reach out or clarify concerns
propositions.quote: this is not the situation that arises in this case

paragraphs.summary: The court finds officers have no obligation to clarify deficient applications absent credibility concerns, citing Solopova and Yuzer, and this case does not require such outreach.

propositions.text: Applicants’ procedural unfairness claim has no merit
propositions.quote: I see no merit in the Applicants’ suggestion that the decisions rejecting their applications were procedurally unfair

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Applicants’ procedural unfairness claim lacks merit.

propositions.text: Applicants must satisfy officer they meet legislative requirements including leaving Canada after authorized stay
propositions.quote: applicants must satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements of the legislative regime; most notably that they will leave Canada at the end of their period of authorized stay

propositions.text: IRPR paragraph 216(1)(b) and Patel confirm this requirement
propositions.quote: IRPR paragraph 216(1)(b); Patel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 570 at para 12

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants must meet legislative requirements including leaving Canada, citing IRPR and Patel.

propositions.text: Applicants must demonstrate sufficient financial resources; officer shall not issue permit unless satisfied
propositions.quote: applicants have a fundamental duty to provide sufficient evidence to support a study permit application

propositions.text: IRPR section 220 mandates financial resources; De La Cruz Garcia and Bestar confirm duty to provide evidence
propositions.quote: an officer “shall not” issue a study permit unless they are satisfied of the Applicant’s financial resources: IRPR section 220. Moreover, applicants have a fundamental duty to provide sufficient evidence to support a study permit application: De La Cruz Garcia v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 784 at paras 8-12; Bestar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 483 at para 12)

paragraphs.summary: The court explains applicants must prove sufficient financial resources under IRPR section 220, citing De La Cruz Garcia and Bestar.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably found Applicants failed to prove sufficient financial resources
propositions.quote: the Officer reasonably found that the Applicants failed to establish that they had sufficient and available financial resources to fund the Principal Applicant’s studies

propositions.text: Reasonableness of this finding dictates dismissal of application
propositions.quote: the reasonableness of this aspect of the decision dictates that this application must be dismissed

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer reasonably concluded insufficient financial resources and dismisses the application accordingly.

propositions.text: Applicants submitted various financial documents including bank statements and tuition deposit
propositions.quote: Applicants submitted bank statements for both the Principal and Associate Applicants, land transfer and title documents, pay slips, a car deed, and a tuition deposit receipt for $7,751.85

propositions.text: Applicants argue their financial info cumulatively met IRPR section 220 requirements and Officer was unreasonable
propositions.quote: Applicants argue that, cumulatively, the financial information they provided satisfied the requirements of section 220 of the IRPR and it was unreasonable for the Officer to find otherwise

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Applicants’ argument
propositions.quote: For the below reasons, I disagree

paragraphs.summary: Applicants submitted financial documents and argue they met requirements; court disagrees with their argument.

propositions.text: Officer’s concern was lack of detailed bank statements verifying fund movement, not fund quantity
propositions.quote: Officer did not express specific concerns with the quantity of funds set out in the documents, but rather with the lack of detailed bank statements and transactions to verify the movement of funds

propositions.text: Applicants say bank statements were like GICs with no regular transactions, so Officer required impossibility
propositions.quote: Applicants stated that the bank statements they provided were for accounts similar to a Guaranteed Investment Certificate (GIC), which do not permit regular transactions. As such, the Applicants assert that the Officer required of them an impossibility

propositions.text: Court rejects Applicants’ argument
propositions.quote: I do not accept this argument

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Officer concerned about lack of transaction details; Applicants say statements were like GICs; court rejects this argument.

propositions.text: Officers must analyze source, nature, stability of funds under IRPR section 220
propositions.quote: officers must conduct an analysis about the source, origin, nature, and stability of applicants’ funds to determine if they are able to defray the cost of their stay in Canada

propositions.text: Aghvamiamoli confirms this analysis requirement at para 28
propositions.quote: Aghvamiamoli v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 1613 [Aghvamiamoli] at para 28

propositions.text: Applicants did not provide statements with detailed transactions or explain nature of accounts
propositions.quote: Applicants did not provide any information related to such accounts, and nor did they provide any explanation to the Officer as to the nature of the accounts for which they did provide information

propositions.text: Applicants are professionals with regular income and presumably have accounts with transactions
propositions.quote: The Applicants are both professionals with regular income; they presumably have expenses that are paid from bank accounts and salaries that are paid into them

propositions.text: Applicants should have provided statements with transactions or explanations
propositions.quote: If they did not, however, it was incumbent on the Applicants to provide statements from accounts that do contain such transactions

paragraphs.summary: The court states officers must analyze fund source and stability; Applicants failed to provide transactional statements or explanations despite regular income.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably concluded Applicants failed IRPR section 220 requirements without sufficient info
propositions.quote: it was reasonable for the Officer to conclude that the Applicants had not met the requirements of section 220 of the IRPR

propositions.text: Respondent points out tuition cost exceeds Applicants’ combined bank assets and deposit was nominal
propositions.quote: Respondent points out, this is all the more the case, given that the costs for the Principal Applicant’s MBA program were significant and exceeded the Applicants’ combined bank assets. Tuition for the program is $54,975 USD, of which the Applicants had only paid a nominal $7,751.85 deposit

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Officer reasonably concluded Applicants failed financial requirements; Respondent notes tuition exceeds assets and deposit was small.

propositions.text: Applicant asks court to reweigh evidence, which is not court’s role on judicial review
propositions.quote: Applicant is asking the court to arrive at a different conclusion on the very evidence that the Officer considered and found to be insufficient

propositions.text: Reweighing evidence is not court’s role on judicial review per Mohammadi at para 16
propositions.quote: which, as I recently noted in a similar case, is not the role of the Court on judicial review: Mohammadi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 598, at para 16

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Applicant improperly asks it to reweigh evidence, which judicial review forbids, citing Mohammadi.

propositions.text: Public instructions require applicants to provide bank statements spanning several months as proof of financial support
propositions.quote: public instructions applicable to those applying for study permits ask applicants to provide, amongst other things, copies of bank statements spanning several months as proof of financial support

propositions.text: Court has dismissed judicial reviews where applicants failed to follow these instructions
propositions.quote: this Court has dismissed applications for judicial review where visa officers have denied study permits to applicants who had not adhered to these instructions

propositions.text: Recent cases Aghvamiamoli, Salamat, Najaran, Sani, Abdisoufi confirm dismissal for failure to follow instructions
propositions.quote: Aghvamiamoli; Salamat v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 545; Najaran v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 541; Sani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 396 [Sani]; Abdisoufi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 164

paragraphs.summary: The court notes public instructions require bank statements and recent cases dismiss reviews where applicants failed to comply.

propositions.text: Section 220 conditions are mandatory and must be met to approve study permit
propositions.quote: The conditions set out at section 220 of the IRPR are mandatory and go beyond merely paying the tuition fees for the intended program of studies; they must be met in order for an officer to approve a study permit application

propositions.text: Sani confirms mandatory nature of section 220 conditions at paras 25, 33
propositions.quote: Sani at paras 25, 33

propositions.text: Officer’s conclusions on financial support are reasonable and determinative
propositions.quote: I find the Officer’s conclusions in this aspect of the decision are reasonable. This finding is determinative of this application for judicial review

propositions.text: Aghvamiamoli para 36 states lack of financial support alone justifies refusal even if other findings unreasonable
propositions.quote: As Justice Régimbald stated in Aghvamiamoli (at para 36): Nevertheless, even if the Officer’s decision is unreasonable in relation to their conclusions on the significance of the Applicant’s ties to Iran, or on his study plan, on which I do not need to conclude, the Officer’s decision is reasonable in relation to the lack of financial support. That consideration, on its own, is sufficient to justify the Officer’s decision to refuse the Applicant’s application for a study permit

paragraphs.summary: The court finds section 220 conditions mandatory; Officer’s financial support conclusion is reasonable and dispositive, citing Sani and Aghvamiamoli.

propositions.text: Officer did not breach duty of fairness and decision was reasonable
propositions.quote: I find that the Officer who rendered the decision in this matter did not breach the duty of fairness, and that the decision itself was reasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer acted fairly and the decision was reasonable.

propositions.text: Judicial review application dismissed and no question certified for appeal
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question is certified for appeal

propositions.text: No question of general importance proposed or found
propositions.quote: No question of general importance was proposed and I agree none exists

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review and refuses to certify any question for appeal, finding no general importance question.
